cells.tense: Right now you're the one deciding what stays and what gets released, and you're doing it with both hands steady.
cells.ask: offer one ending outward — say what it gave you, out loud, to someone who saw it — so the release comes back as permission to let it rest
cells.core:
Nothing has to be pried out of your grip. The ending and the tending are the same motion, and you can feel that — you let go of what's done and the letting go doesn't cost you anything you still need. You're in the middle of a clearing and you're the one holding the rake.

The next thing this steadiness can take on is a witness. The release is real and it's been quiet — no one has said back to you that the years of carrying were seen. Let it be named, and the completion stops feeling like loss and starts feeling like a finished thing you get to set down.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things and tending things in the same breath.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: where what's finished has to be let go of, so what's next has room

cells.tense: You're already living past the ending — bracing for what should come after, and holding on tighter to keep it from going wrong.
cells.ask: let one thing end without arranging what replaces it, and let the satisfaction that's already here be enough for now — so the vision you make next isn't running on fear
cells.core:
There's a clearing that wants to happen and you're standing in front of it with your arms full, trying to make the next thing exist before this one has finished. The holding is the problem. What you're gripping hasn't asked to be saved, and the effort is spending the care you meant to have for what's next.

At its steadier end, this looks like a garden bed being turned over in autumn — you don't plant through what's still standing, you let it go back in and wait. The satisfaction of that isn't passive; it's knowing what you built was real enough to release. Let one thing finish without you managing the outcome, and the imagining that comes after has something honest to stand on.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding on to make the future happen, and it's costing you the present.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: where what's finished has to be let go of, so what's next has room

cells.tense: Something already ended and you're still standing at the threshold, not having crossed into what it left open.
cells.ask: let one hope about what's next be small and true and yours, and act on just that — hoping again is what refills the part of you that can release
cells.core:
You've been clearing without letting anything be cleared. The ending happened, or the ending is here, and you're not in the room for it — not planting, not releasing, not saying the thing that would mark it done. The care you have for what grows hasn't gone anywhere. It's just not moving through you right now.

As this steadies, it looks like a field after harvest: the stalks are down, the ground is bare, and the farmer is already walking the rows for next year. That walking isn't strain. It's hope with somewhere to go. Let one plan, one seed, one small want be real to you — not the whole field, just one row — and the release comes back on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You're at the edge of the clearing and you haven't stepped in.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: where what's finished has to be let go of, so what's next has room

cells.tense: You're already letting go of what's done and already tending what's next — and you'd say it's just what needed doing.
cells.ask: name one thing you released this year and call it yours — the ending was your choice, and saying so hands the surrender back its dignity
cells.core:
The clearing has been happening. You've been the one doing it — deciding what stays, what gets let go, what gets carried forward — and you've been calling it maintenance, or logistics, or just getting through. But endings are choices, and you've been making them cleanly without giving yourself credit for the decision.

On its steady side, it looks like a kitchen counter cleared at night: the day's work is done, the surfaces are bare, and no one applauds. The person who did it knows. Let one of those releases be spoken — say what it was, who it mattered to, that you chose it — and the letting go stops being a task and becomes something you did on purpose.
cells.sheetLine: You've been ending things and calling it housekeeping.
